title: How Do We Learn by Hector Ruiz Martin 2024
author: G-Rob
source: What I Talk About When I Talk About Education (witawitaeducation.wordpress.com), June 23,
summary: G-Rob reviews Hector Ruiz Martin's How Do We Learn, praising it as an unusually focused and rigorous synthesis of evidence-based education rather than a loosely-themed survey. The review highlights the book's treatment of emotion, motivation, metacognition and social interaction alongside more familiar territory like feedback and assessment, arguing that individual chapters taught the reviewer as much as whole books on the same topics. What stands out most is the book's nuance: rather than delivering dogmatic verdicts, it works through contested areas like cooperative learning, self-control interventions, grades, and growth mindset, reaching qualified conclusions that avoid both credulity and dismissal. G-Rob singles out the chapter on direct instruction versus discovery learning as the clearest treatment of that debate they have encountered, and describes the book as having challenged some of their own prior convictions, particularly a reflexive dislike of grades. The review closes by recommending the book to any teacher willing to read it slowly, one chapter at a time, calling it a strong candidate to become the standard reference text.
points: The review credits the book's power to its refusal to be dogmatic, working through cooperative learning, self-control, and grades to reach qualified rather than sweeping conclusions.
It singles out the book's treatment of direct instruction, discovery learning, and cooperative learning as the clearest discussion of that debate the reviewer has read.
G-Rob reports the book directly changed a personal conviction, softening a previously 'flamboyantly anti-grades' stance after reading the evidence presented.
The review recommends slow, chapter-at-a-time reading rather than a straight read-through, treating the density of the material as a feature, not a flaw.
quotes: This books feels significant. Many books try to cover the breadth of educational science gathered round a theme, a thread that pulls them together.
Not a word is wasted, chapters on aspects of teaching (such as feedback or assessment) taught me as much as whole books on the topics had done.
The nuanced discussions of complex issues. Martin reviewed the science related to key topics and pulled out the key findings (or “best bets” as others have labelled them) with exceptional clarity.
It didn’t rule out the benefits of cooperative learning, instead it made clear that the focus should be on assessing the outcome (individuals learning) and not the product.
It also challenged my prejudices. I have been flamboyantly anti-grades. But the book carefully explained where they are beneficial.
It also wasn’t afraid to tackle the scientific backing of some controversial theories such as growth mindset and grit.
Overall, an outstanding summary of where we are with evidence-based teaching. It should become the go to text.
